Compose already reverses funcs to apply left-to-right? Wait Compose __init__ reverses funcs: funcs = tuple(reversed(funcs)). So if we pass (f, g, h) to Compose, first becomes h, funcs = (f,g). Then __call__ calls first(*args) then f, g. So order: h(f(g(x)))? Let's test mentally: Suppose Compose(funcs) with funcs=(f,g,h). reversed -> (h,g,f). first = h, funcs = (g,f). call: ret = h(*args); then ret = g(ret); then ret = f(ret). So order: f(g(h(x))). That is left-to-right? Wait original description: compose(f,g,h)(x,y) = f(g(h(x,y))) if functions applied right-to-left. Compose is defined to achieve that: we pass (f,g,h) and get f(g(h(x,y))). That matches docstring. Good.

compose_left should produce left-to-right: first function applied first then next etc. So we can implement as Compose reversed order of funcs? Let's check: if we want compose_left(f,g,h)(x) = h(g(f(x)))? Wait left-to-right: first f, then g, then h. So result: h(g(f(x)))? Wait compute: start x, apply f -> f(x), then g -> g(f(x)), then h -> h(g(f(x))). So final is h(g(f(x))). Right-to-left compose gives f(g(h(x))). So compose_left should call Compose with funcs reversed order: i.e., Compose(funcs[::-1])? Let's test: Suppose funcs=(f,g,h). Compose(funcs[::-1]) -> Compose((h,g,f)). reversed inside Compose -> (f,g,h). first = f, funcs = (g,h). call: ret = f(x); ret = g(f(x)); ret = h(g(f(x))). This yields left-to-right. So compose_left can just return Compose(funcs[::-1]). But we need to preserve behavior when no funcs: identity. Implementation: if not funcs: return identity. If len==1: return funcs[0]. else return Compose(funcs[::-1]). But Compose expects tuple; we pass reversed. Let's implement.
